notes.title: Start here: a cooking journal and its request boundary
notes.body:
Recipe Lab is a single-user cooking journal: a **dish** has **recipes**, and a recipe has **cook logs** (each time you cooked it). The server is only four files, and the course is about the **request boundary**: what the server checks before it lets a request write anything.

Reading order:

1. `astraupskill/01-CODEBASE-MAP.md`: the four server files in one table, the data model, and one request traced end to end. Its "Where to read first" list is the best way into the code.
2. `02-CONCEPTS.md`: six numbered concepts, each tied to line numbers.
3. `03-WORKED-CHANGE.md`: the `h()` wrapper and `validatePayload` line by line, and the four tests annotated.
4. `04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md` and `05-PRACTICE.md`.
5. `06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md`: answers and eleven senior review findings.

Read the server before any React. The map says all writes live in `server/index.ts`, so most questions point into that file.

excerpts.quote: Recipe Lab is a single-user, local cooking journal: Dish → Recipe → Cook Log. The improvement this course studies is the **request boundary**
The server is four files. Learn their roles before reading any React.

readMore.why: The file table, data model, and the order to read the code.
The six concepts behind the questions.

notes.title: Concept: what h() and validatePayload do before a handler runs
notes.body:
Every route is wrapped in a function called `h()`. Before your handler code runs, `h()` does three things:

1. Checks every route parameter whose name ends in `id`: digits only, a safe integer, at least 1. Anything else is a 400.
2. Rewrites that id into a plain canonical number string.
3. For POST and PATCH (except the photo upload route), calls `validatePayload(req.body)`.

If any of these throws, `fail()` answers and the handler never starts, so nothing is written.

`validatePayload` is an **allow-list**: it checks the keys it knows about (names, titles, tags, yield, ingredients, steps). The worked-change chapter is explicit about two consequences you should keep in mind while reading the rest: keys it does not know are not checked at all, and `h()` checks the shape of an id but never whether the record exists. Each handler must do that itself.

excerpts.quote: ["POST", "PATCH"].includes(req.method) && !req.path.endsWith("/photos") ) validatePayload(req.body);
It checks **only keys it knows**. Unknown keys pass through (and are ignored by handlers).

readMore.why: The wrapper, the validator and fail(), explained line by line.

notes.title: Concept: one value, many representations
notes.body:
The codebase map gives a reading technique worth using everywhere: at each function boundary, note the value coming in, the value going out, and any side effect. Watch especially for **representation changes**, because that is where bugs cluster.

Examples from this app:

- A quantity is a string in the editor, a number or null on the wire, and a REAL column in SQLite. NULL deliberately means "to taste".
- A route id is a string in `req.params` until it is converted to a number.
- `cooked_on` is a `YYYY-MM-DD` calendar label, not a timestamp.
- Search is a second copy of the data: an FTS5 table that the handlers rebuild themselves. It is not a foreign-key target, so deleting rows elsewhere does not clean it up automatically.

Several quiz questions are really asking "what representation is this value in at this moment, and who converts it?"

excerpts.quote: Watch for **representation changes**: the quantity is a string in the editor (`RecipeEditor.tsx:9`), a `number | null` on the wire, and a `REAL` in SQLite
`search_index` is a virtual table, **not** a foreign-key target, so deleting a dish does not remove its search rows.

readMore.why: Search as a second representation of the same data.

notes.title: Why deleting a missing cook log still returns 204
notes.body:
The cook-log DELETE handler converts the id, runs a transaction that deletes photo files, search rows and the cook-log row, then always answers 204. It never checks that the log existed. `h()` only checks that the id **looks** like a positive whole number; existence is each handler's job, and the delete handlers skip it. Deleting zero rows is not an error in SQL, so 99999 quietly returns **204**. The review lists this as finding 5: typos are invisible.

Why the others are wrong:
- **400, larger than any id**: `h()` validates shape, not whether the number is in the table.
- **500, zero rows affected**: a DELETE that matches nothing succeeds in SQLite; nothing throws.
- **404, h() looks the record up**: the worked change says plainly that `h()` does not check existence.

excerpts.quote: db.prepare("DELETE FROM cook_logs WHERE id = ?").run(id); }); res.status(204).end();

Note what `h()` does **not** do: it does not check that the record exists. Each handler does that itself (e.g. `:147-149`, `:320-322`) — and the DELETE handlers do not, so deleting a missing id returns 204.

notes.title: The one route that skips payload validation
notes.body:
This is a goal-check question: each exercise in the guide pairs a Goal with a Check, and the wrong choices are the Checks of other exercises in the same guide.

The Goal is to find the route that skips `validatePayload`. Look at the condition in `h()`: it validates POST and PATCH bodies **unless** `req.path.endsWith("/photos")`. So `POST /api/logs/:id/photos` is skipped. The reason is that a photo upload is a multipart form body, not a JSON object, so a JSON validator would make no sense there. The Check asks you to name that route, point at the exclusion, and give that reason.

Why the other Checks belong elsewhere:
- "(a) ... (d) write a file:line answer" is the first exercise, locating ownership.
- "a search for INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE in server/queries.ts" is the third exercise, proving `queries.ts` is read-only.

excerpts.quote: !req.path.endsWith("/photos")
**Check:** you can name `POST /api/logs/:id/photos` and point at the `/photos` exclusion in `server/index.ts:86-88`, and explain why (multipart bodies are not JSON objects).

notes.title: Explaining the cook-log title denormalisation
notes.body:
This is a goal-check question: each exercise in the guide pairs a Goal with a Check, and the wrong choices are the Checks of other exercises in the same guide.

A **denormalisation** is when you copy data into another place instead of looking it up. Here a cook log's search title is built as the recipe title plus the cook date, on `server/db.ts:101`. Because the recipe title is copied in, renaming a recipe must rebuild every cook log under it; that is why `reindexRecipeTree` exists. Dish names are not copied into cook-log titles, so a dish rename only re-indexes the dish row. The Check asks you to name that line and predict that no cook-log title changes on a dish rename.

Why the other Checks belong elsewhere:
- "make_again: sometimes ... server/index.ts:56-57" is the "classify a field" exercise.
- "ingredient count after PATCH ..." is the "three ingredients cases" exercise.

excerpts.quote: `${l.recipe_title} — ${l.cooked_on}`
/** Reindex a recipe and every cook log under it (titles embed the recipe name). */ export function reindexRecipeTree(recipeId: number) {
you can name the exact line (`server/db.ts:101`) that forces `reindexRecipeTree`

notes.title: Validate before the DELETE, not after it
notes.body:
`writeRecipeChildren` replaces ingredients wholesale. When `body.ingredients` is an array, its very first action is `DELETE FROM ingredients WHERE recipe_id = ?`, and only then does it insert the new rows. If validation happened inside that function after the delete, one bad row (say a negative quantity) would be found only after every valid ingredient was already gone. So validation runs earlier, in `h()`, before the handler is even called; a rejected body writes nothing.

Why the others are wrong:
- **only for performance**: the concepts chapter gives a correctness reason: a typo would wipe a valid recipe.
- **needs the old ingredient ids**: `validatePayload` only looks at the request body; it never reads the database.
- **node:sqlite cannot roll back a DELETE**: it can; `tx()` issues ROLLBACK on any throw. The design avoids relying on that.

excerpts.quote: if (Array.isArray(body?.ingredients)) { db.prepare("DELETE FROM ingredients WHERE recipe_id = ?").run(recipeId);
If `validatePayload` ran after line 235, a typo would wipe an otherwise valid recipe. It runs in `h()` (`:85-89`), before the handler is even called.

notes.title: Cook-log fields are normalised, not rejected
notes.body:
`validatePayload` only covers dish and recipe fields. Cook-log fields never reach a rejection branch; instead the handler cleans them up. `rating()` rounds and then clamps to the range 1 to 5, so 9 becomes **5**. `str()` returns the trimmed text only if the value is a string, otherwise the fallback `""`, so the number 42 becomes **an empty string**. Nothing tells the caller; the review calls this silent data loss (finding 3).

Why the others are wrong:
- **a 400**: cook-log keys are not in `validatePayload`'s list at all.
- **9 and "42"**: `rating` clamps, and `str` does not convert numbers to text.
- **both null**: `rating` returns null only for a missing or non-numeric value; 9 is a number. `str` falls back to `""`, not null.

excerpts.quote: const str = (v: unknown, fallback = ""): string => typeof v === "string" ? v.trim() : fallback;
return Math.min(5, Math.max(1, Math.round(n)));
`validatePayload` covers dish and recipe fields only; cook-log fields never reach a rejection branch.

notes.title: Files on disk are outside the transaction
notes.body:
A database transaction can undo database changes, but it cannot undo deleting a file. The cook-log delete calls `fs.rm` on each photo file **inside** `tx()`, before the rows are deleted. If something later in that transaction throws, `tx()` rolls the rows back, but the files are already gone. You are left with photo rows that point at missing files. Dish and recipe deletes avoid this by collecting filenames inside the transaction and removing the files only after it commits. That is review finding 1.

Why the others are wrong:
- **SQLite locks the files**: SQLite has no idea the photo files exist; only filenames are stored.
- **files never deleted on rollback**: the `fs.rm` calls are made before any rollback could happen; a rollback does not cancel them.
- **async, so it always runs after commit**: async only means the callback finishes later; the deletion is started inside the transaction and is not tied to the commit.

excerpts.quote: tx(() => { // Photo rows cascade, but the files on disk won't remove themselves.
fs.rm(path.join(PHOTO_DIR, p.filename), { force: true }, () => {});
Cook-log delete removes photo **files** inside the transaction; a rollback would leave rows pointing at deleted files.

notes.title: Why isDate round-trips through toISOString
notes.body:
`isDate` has three checks. The pattern only says "four digits, dash, two digits, dash, two digits". `Date.parse` is lenient: for "2026-02-30" JavaScript does not fail, it rolls over into March. The third check turns the parsed date back into an ISO string and requires it to equal the input. "2026-02-30" comes back as "2026-03-02", which is not equal, so it is **rejected** instead of silently becoming a different day. `cooked_on` is a calendar label, so it must stay exactly what was typed.

Why the others are wrong:
- **convert local date to UTC before storing**: nothing is converted; the check only compares, and the original string is what gets stored.
- **Date.parse is NaN before 1970**: it handles such dates; that is not the reason.
- **strip a time Date.parse appends**: `Date.parse` returns a number, not a string; the `slice(0, 10)` is there to compare just the date part.

excerpts.quote: const isDate = (s: string) => /^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/.test(s) && Number.isFinite(Date.parse(s)) && new Date(s).toISOString().slice(0, 10) === s;
`cooked_on` is a calendar label, not an instant; `isDate` (`:59-62`) round-trips through `toISOString()` so `2026-02-30` is rejected rather than rolled over to March.

notes.title: Proving queries.ts never writes
notes.body:
This is a goal-check question: each exercise in the guide pairs a Goal with a Check, and the wrong choices are the Checks of other exercises in the same guide.

The Goal is to prove that `server/queries.ts` is read-only. The simplest proof is a text search: every write in SQL is an `INSERT`, `UPDATE` or `DELETE` statement, so if a search for those three words in that file finds nothing, the file cannot be writing. The codebase map backs this up: all writes live in `server/index.ts`.

Why the other Checks belong elsewhere:
- "(a) ... (d) write a file:line answer" is the first exercise, locating ownership.
- "name POST /api/logs/:id/photos ..." is the second exercise, the route that skips validation.

excerpts.quote: **Check:** a search for `INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE` in `server/queries.ts` finds zero matches.
Important: **all writes live in `server/index.ts`**. `queries.ts` has no update functions

notes.title: Omitted ingredients versus an empty list
notes.body:
`writeRecipeChildren` only touches ingredients when `Array.isArray(body?.ingredients)` is true.

- `PATCH {title:"x"}` has no `ingredients` key, so the check is false and the existing 2 rows are untouched: **2**.
- `PATCH {ingredients: []}` is an array, so the DELETE runs and the insert loop runs zero times: **0**. The concepts table calls this intentional: an empty list means "remove them all".

Why the others are wrong:
- **2, then a 400**: an empty array is valid; `validatePayload` only rejects non-arrays, too many rows or bad rows.
- **2, then 2**: that would treat `[]` like an omitted key, but an empty array is still an array.
- **0, then 0**: omitting the key does not delete anything; test 1 relies on that.

excerpts.quote: if (Array.isArray(body?.ingredients)) { db.prepare("DELETE FROM ingredients WHERE recipe_id = ?").run(recipeId);
| no `ingredients` key | `Array.isArray` is false (`:234`) | Existing rows untouched | | `ingredients: []` | Array, loop runs zero times | All ingredients removed — intentional |

notes.title: Validated is not the same as canonical
notes.body:
Before the fix, `h()` checked that "01" was digits, a safe integer and at least 1, and it passed. But it left `req.params.id` as the raw text "01". A handler comparing ids as text would then disagree with SQLite's integer id 1. The fix is one line that rewrites the parameter to `String(Number(value))`. The lesson the worked change draws: checking a value's shape and converting it into one standard form are two separate steps, and it is easy to forget the second once the first passes.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Express strips zeros on GET**: Express does not change parameter text at all.
- **SQLite stores ids as text**: ids are integers; the risk was handler code comparing text, not duplicate rows.
- **the regex rejects leading zeros**: `/^\d+$/` accepts "01"; it only requires digits.

excerpts.quote: // Canonicalize so handlers compare an integer, not the raw text ("01" -> "1"). if (key.toLowerCase().endsWith("id")) req.params[key] = String(Number(value));
Lesson: validating a shape and normalising a value are two steps, and the second is easy to forget once the first passes.

notes.title: A misspelled field slips past an allow-list
notes.body:
`validatePayload` checks ingredient rows key by key, but only the keys it knows: `item`, `unit`, `note`, `section` and `qty`. `quantity` is not one of them, so it is never looked at, and the row passes. The request is a valid array, so `writeRecipeChildren` deletes the old ingredients and inserts one Salt row; its `qty` is NULL because no `qty` was sent. Result: **200**, with the list replaced. The worked change flags this exact trap.

Why the others are wrong:
- **400 like qty**: the negative check reads `row.qty`, which is undefined here.
- **400 for unknown keys**: unknown keys pass through; the validator is an allow-list of checks, not a reject-unknown filter.
- **200 but old rows kept**: any array of ingredients triggers the wholesale replacement.

excerpts.quote: row.qty !== undefined && row.qty !== null &&

`{ "item": "Salt", "quantity": -1 }` is **accepted** — `validatePayload` ignores unknown keys, so the request succeeds with 200 and *replaces* the recipe's ingredient list with one `Salt` row whose `qty` is `NULL`.

notes.title: Why a recipe rename cascades but a dish rename does not
notes.body:
A cook log's search title is stored as the recipe title plus the cook date. That copy is a denormalisation: when the recipe is renamed, every cook log's stored title is now stale, so the recipe PATCH calls `reindexRecipeTree` to rebuild them. Dish names are not copied into those titles. Wherever the dish name is shown in search results, it is looked up live at query time, so renaming a dish only needs to rebuild the dish's own search row.

Why the others are wrong:
- **dishes have no search rows**: `search_index` holds three kinds of rows, and dishes are one; the dish PATCH calls `reindexDish`.
- **skipped for performance**: the code comment gives the real reason: nothing needs it.
- **FTS5 triggers**: the schema deliberately uses no triggers; handlers re-index by hand.

excerpts.quote: `${l.recipe_title} — ${l.cooked_on}`
// Cook-log search titles don't embed the dish name, but recipe context // strings resolve live, so only the dish row needs reindexing here.
triggers, because a recipe's searchable body spans four source tables.

notes.title: localhost in a log line is not a security setting
notes.body:
The startup message prints `http://localhost:5274`, but that is just text. What decides who can connect is the `app.listen` call, and it passes only a port, no host. When Node is given no host, it listens on every network interface. There is no authentication either. So **anyone on the network who can reach port 5274** can read and change the journal. The review says binding to `127.0.0.1` is the first change before running it anywhere else.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Express refuses non-loopback connections**: Express has no such default; it accepts whatever the socket accepts.
- **only this machine, since the URL says localhost**: the URL is printed, not enforced.
- **only the Vite CORS origin**: CORS is a browser rule; it does not stop other clients such as curl from connecting.

excerpts.quote: app.listen(PORT, () => { console.log(`  Recipe Lab API  →  http://localhost:${PORT}`);
`app.listen(PORT)` (`server/index.ts:597`) passes no host, so Node binds every interface, not just `localhost`.

notes.title: Classifying make_again: normalised to NULL
notes.body:
This is a goal-check question: each exercise in the guide pairs a Goal with a Check, and the wrong choices are the Checks of other exercises in the same guide.

"Classify a field" means: decide whether the code **rejects** a bad value (validation) or **converts** it (normalisation). For `make_again`, the deciding line is the `makeAgain` helper. If the value is one of the allowed `MAKE_AGAIN` options it is kept, otherwise it becomes `null`. So "sometimes" is not rejected; it is quietly stored as NULL. The Check asks for that line and that stored value.

Why the other Checks belong elsewhere:
- "ingredient count after PATCH ..." is the "three ingredients cases" exercise.
- "name the exact line server/db.ts:101 ..." is the "explain a denormalisation" exercise.

excerpts.quote: const makeAgain = (v: unknown): MakeAgain | null => MAKE_AGAIN.includes(v as MakeAgain) ? (v as MakeAgain) : null;
Validation rejects; normalisation converts.

notes.title: The three ingredients cases, and where to confirm them
notes.body:
This is a goal-check question: each exercise in the guide pairs a Goal with a Check, and the wrong choices are the Checks of other exercises in the same guide.

The Goal is to predict what happens to a recipe's ingredients in the three cases from the concepts table. The Check gives the counts for a recipe with 2 ingredients: omitted key leaves 2; an empty list leaves 0; a row with a negative `qty` is rejected with 400 before anything is deleted, so 2 remain. It then asks you to confirm against the "invalid edits change nothing" test, which snapshots the recipe and checks it is unchanged after bad PATCHes.

Why the other Checks belong elsewhere:
- "make_again: sometimes ..." is the "classify a field" exercise.
- "name the exact line server/db.ts:101 ..." is the "explain a denormalisation" exercise.

excerpts.quote: for a recipe with 2 ingredients, write the ingredient count after PATCH `{title:"x"}` (2), PATCH `{ingredients:[]}` (0), and PATCH `{ingredients:[{item:"a",qty:-1}]}` (2, status 400).
| `ingredients: [{item:"Salt",qty:-1}]` | Rejected earlier by `validatePayload` (`:645-655`) | 400, nothing deleted |

notes.title: Why the simple tx() helper is safe only here
notes.body:
`tx(fn)` is BEGIN, run `fn`, COMMIT, or ROLLBACK and rethrow. It is safe here because `node:sqlite`'s `DatabaseSync` is **synchronous** and there is **one connection**. `fn` cannot `await`, so no other request can run in the middle of the transaction. With an async driver like `pg`, other requests could interleave while you wait, and they would share the connection; the same helper would need a dedicated client for each transaction.

Why the others are wrong:
- **SQLite serialises writes, so no transaction is needed**: the transaction is what makes the parent update, child replacement and re-index all-or-nothing.
- **PostgreSQL cannot ROLLBACK in try/catch**: it can; the problem is which connection the statements run on.
- **re-entrant on SQLite**: it is not re-entrant on SQLite either; a nested call would issue a second BEGIN and throw.

excerpts.quote: export function tx<T>(fn: () => T): T { db.exec('BEGIN'); try { const out = fn(); db.exec('COMMIT'); return out; } catch (err) { db.exec('ROLLBACK');

`DatabaseSync` is **synchronous**. `fn` cannot `await`, so no other request can run between `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` in this process. With an async driver (e.g. `pg`), the same helper would need a dedicated client per transaction.
`tx` is **not re-entrant**: calling `tx` inside `tx` would issue a second `BEGIN` and SQLite would throw

notes.title: How toFtsQuery shapes a search
notes.body:
`toFtsQuery` trims the input, splits it on whitespace, removes double quotes, and drops empty pieces. Then it wraps **each** term in double quotes, and adds `*` only after the **last** one. For "half-and-half cre" that gives `"half-and-half" "cre"*`. Quoting stops FTS5 from reading the hyphens (or an apostrophe in "don't") as query syntax. The trailing `*` makes the last word a prefix, so "cre" matches "cream" while you are still typing.

Why the others are wrong:
- **one quoted phrase**: the input is split, and each term is quoted separately.
- **split on hyphens, star on every term**: it splits only on whitespace (`/\s+/`), and only the last term gets `*`.
- **raw text to MATCH**: that is what the quoting exists to prevent.

excerpts.quote: .split(/\s+/) .map((t) => t.replace(/"/g, '').trim())
return terms.map((t, i) => (i === terms.length - 1 ? `"${t}"*` : `"${t}"`)).join(' ');
